comments.text:
Created attachment 3156
Alternative `which()` algorithm

I've implemented an alternative algorithm for `which()` which uses less memory and is often faster (up to 3x in some cases).

If you prefer to see it on GitHub, it lives here:

https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/pull/117

Otherwise, it is attached as a patch.

You'll notice that I've allocated a `bool` array using `R_alloc()`. I figured that using `bool` was okay since R-admin now states that C99 is required to compile R, and that should be enough to give us access to `bool` (we've also been using `bool` in vctrs and dplyr for quite a while with no issues).

https://github.com/wch/r-source/commit/3d6f56e87b82a0a0b55f7b83a94c70d1f26fd578#diff-dc3a9172fa37909f89ff6dc9c8c20ac1a45ada83a8db6e1de1154c5198909d0aR1138

The implementation first counts up the number of `TRUE` elements and also tracks whether or not the `i`th element is `TRUE` or not inside the bool array. Then it allocates an output of the right size using the count, and fills it where the bool array is `true`.

Previously, an integer/double vector of the full size of `x` was being allocated, and it seemed to me that we could be less memory intensive by using the bool array without any downsides.

I've ensured that this algorithm is still ALTREP friendly by keeping `ITERATE_BY_REGION()`. We could in theory avoid the `bool` array entirely by calling `ITERATE_BY_REGION()` twice (first loop computes the total size, then allocate the output, then the second loop fills the output), but I was worried about the case of an ALTREP logical vector that might have an expensive `Get_region` or `Elt` method, and the `bool` array approach didn't seem to be any slower.

The real win in performance comes from writing the algorithm in a completely branchless way. `which()` is naturally a "jumpy" function since if the `i`th element is `FALSE`, there is typically nothing that says the `i+1`th element is also `FALSE`, so getting rid of any branches seems to help a decent bit here. Generally, the more equal the mix of `TRUE` and `FALSE` (and `NA`) is, the more dramatic the increase in performance is over the original approach.

The only time I have seen a decrease in performance is when the distribution is _heavily_ skewed towards `FALSE`, like 96%+ `FALSE`. But that difference in performance rapidly closes as the percent `FALSE` decreases, and, as you'll see in my benchmarks below, once you get down to 90% `FALSE` we've already flipped to the new algorithm being faster, and it continues to be faster for all other cases. And, of course, the new algorithm is more memory friendly for all cases.

The absolute values of the timings below may vary of course, but I hope that the relative differences are stable. For reference, I am on a 2018 Macbook Pro that still has an Intel chip. I have a feeling that absolute timings on the Apple M1/M2 chips will be much faster than mine, but again, hopefully the relative difference of the approaches holds.

The proposal by Suharto is more minimal but doesn't reduce the amount of memory used by `which()`, which I do think would be a useful feature.

Here's a few more benchmarks. Nothing looks _dramatically_ different between the two (maybe 15% either way depending on the data). The fact that the new approach uses 30-50% less memory without speed tradeoff is pretty nice though. And I still think that the benchmarks with random data (shown above) are likely more representable of a typical call to `which()`, which shows dramatically larger speedups with the new approach.

comments.text:
The above timings and memory improvements are still valid for current R-devel 90193.

The branchless patch is simpler, and provides real speedup for the randomized logical vector case, but does not improve memory usage. (Note: I couldn't apply the branchless patch directly, perhaps due to some divergence since 2023, but it's easy enough to make the changes manually. I'll attach a new version of this patch for reference.)

The alternative which() implementation provided by Davis improves speed in the randomized case and real memory improvements. The code makes sense to me.

All tests pass locally, and I built and checked a small selection of CRAN packages: __abind__, __bit64__, __data.table__, __dplyr__, and __stringi__. These also passed. That's about as far as I can take this without input from R-core.

Further details here: https://github.com/r-devel/r-dev-day/issues/158
